source: Evans & Stanovich (2013) Dual-process theories of higher cognition: advancing the debate
finding: The two authors drop the old long feature lists (fast/slow, associative/rule-based, and so on). Only two features define the types. Type 1 is autonomous: it needs no working memory and fires when its trigger appears. Type 2 needs working memory and can sustain cognitive decoupling (holding a hypothetical apart from the real).
numbers: Eight binary features would give 64 cells; the authors say real theories need only 2 of them ('2 cells out of 64'), so correlated features such as speed are not defining.
quote: Our view of the literature is that autonomous processing is the defining feature of Type 1 processing.
limits: Position paper that answers critics. It reports no new experiment. Speed, load and accuracy are only correlated with the types.
agent_relevance: Define our two modes by function, not by speed: a cheap autonomous pass versus a pass that holds a hypothetical (a candidate answer, a counterexample) and tests it. Do not use 'fast' as the switch.

source: Evans & Stanovich (2013) Dual-process theories of higher cognition: advancing the debate
finding: Default-interventionist (DI) theory: Type 1 gives a default answer quickly and Type 2 may or may not step in. Parallel-competitive theory (Sloman 1996, Smith & DeCoster 2000): both run at once and conflict is resolved. The authors argue for DI because Type 2 uses scarce working memory and Type 1 is far faster, so a parallel design makes the fast process wait for the slow one.
numbers: Intervention is predicted when difficulty, novelty and motivation together call on working memory. Most behaviour follows the default.
limits: The argument is conceptual. Later data (Trippas et al. 2017; Bago & De Neys 2017) challenge strict DI.
agent_relevance: The schema's default-then-check structure (S3 generate, S4 test) is the DI form. Intervention should be triggered by conflict or novelty signals, which matches guardrail G1.

source: Evans & Stanovich (2013) Dual-process theories of higher cognition: advancing the debate
finding: Evidence for two types comes from three methods: (1) manipulations that push one type (instructions, working-memory load, speeded tasks); (2) neuroimaging; (3) psychometrics (Type 2 performance correlates with intelligence, Type 1 does not). Load and speeding give opposite effects on accuracy and on belief bias, not just random error.
numbers: Examples as reported: De Neys (2006) found Linda conjunction fallacy errors come faster than correct answers and correct answers drop under load; matching bias on the Wason selection task rises under speeding (Roberts & Newton 2001) and under load.
limits: Second-hand summary of studies. The authors predict exceptions: when pragmatic cues make the right answer easy, intelligence does not predict it.
agent_relevance: A load or time cap on the first pass is a valid way to read what the model's 'intuition' is. We can compare a cheap-pass answer with a long-pass answer item by item.

source: Evans & Stanovich (2013) Dual-process theories of higher cognition: advancing the debate
finding: Both authors say it is a fallacy that Type 1 is always wrong and Type 2 always right. Type 1 fails mostly in 'hostile' environments with misleading cues. Feeling of rightness (Thompson 2011) is named as a driver of whether people override: confident intuitions are rethought less.
numbers: Cited: confidence is unrelated to accuracy on some tasks (Shynkaruk & Thompson 2006), yet it still controls rethinking.
limits: Confidence driving rethinking is documented for humans. For LLMs it is untested here.
agent_relevance: Do not treat the quick pass as the biased one by definition. Gate on checkable signals, not on the label 'fast'. Model self-confidence is a weak gate (see G10).

source: Osman (2004) An evaluation of dual-process theories of reasoning
finding: The main early critique. Osman describes three dual theories: Evans & Over (1996) (System 1 implicit, associative, fast; System 2 explicit, sequential, working-memory heavy; two kinds of rationality), Sloman (1996) (associative versus rule-based, a computational split; Smolensky-style connectionist base versus symbolic rules) and Stanovich & West (2000). She argues one graded system can explain the same data.
numbers: Review covering the Wason selection task, the conjunction fallacy and belief-bias syllogisms (23 pages).
limits: A single-system alternative, not a full replacement model. Later work (Evans & Stanovich 2013) says the critique attacks the whole class and assumes all features must align.
agent_relevance: Treat the S1/S2 labels as a useful handle, not a proven architecture. The schema's note 'the split is contested' stands.

source: Osman (2004) An evaluation of dual-process theories of reasoning
finding: Sloman's Criterion S: a result counts as evidence for two systems only if two answers conflict at once, one felt strongly even when the other is known to be right. Standard example: people keep the conjunction fallacy after learning the rule. Osman notes that informed groups do not escape it, and argues a single graded associative account can also explain this.
numbers: Tversky & Kahneman (1974, 1983) as cited: naive, informed and sophisticated groups violated the conjunction rule 85%-89% of the time.
limits: Secondary report of the figures.
agent_relevance: A model can 'know' a rule and still output the heuristic answer. Do not assume that stating the rule fixes the answer; run the check.

source: Osman (2004) An evaluation of dual-process theories of reasoning
finding: On belief-bias syllogisms the evidence suggests that people start with some analytic work and that the bias sits at evaluation. That conflicts with Sloman's picture where fast belief precedes analysis. Newstead et al. (1992) found support for mental models: people evaluated the argument but did not look for counterexamples when the conclusion was indeterminate.
numbers: Evans & Pollard (1990) pattern cited: believable conclusions accepted after a quick check.
limits: Narrative review. No effect sizes in the passages read.
agent_relevance: Even the 'intuitive' path includes some analysis. Our test step should look for a counterexample, since failure to search for one is where bias comes from.

source: Frederick (2005) Cognitive reflection and decision making
finding: Introduces the 3-item Cognitive Reflection Test (bat and ball, 5 machines, lily pads). Each item has a strong wrong first answer (10, 100, 24). Among all wrong answers the posited intuitive one dominates; correct solvers often crossed out the intuitive answer first, never the other way round.
numbers: 3,428 respondents in 35 studies over 26 months. Mean score by site: MIT 2.18 (N=61; 7% scored 0, 16% one, 30% two, 48% three), Princeton 1.63 (N=121; 18% / 27% / 28% / 26%), Toledo 0.57. Sex difference: men 1.47, women 1.03.
quote: ability or disposition to resist reporting the response that first comes to mind
limits: Mostly selective-college samples; the author says group gaps are understated. The task mixes reflection with maths skill (see a11).
agent_relevance: The CRT is a proxy for 'does the model override its first impulse'. For LLMs, CRT-like items are likely in training data, so scores are contaminated.

source: Frederick (2005) Cognitive reflection and decision making
finding: CRT score predicted patience and risk choices. High scorers (3 of 3) were more patient, and more willing to gamble when the gamble had higher expected value. The effect on time preference was stronger for women, the effect on risk was stronger for men.
numbers: Direction only was read from the text; the table cells for each choice were scrambled in the PDF text, so exact percentages are not recorded.
limits: The CRT also correlates with other cognitive tests, so predicting choice does not isolate reflection.
agent_relevance: Success on CRT-type items goes with long-run, expected-value choices. A scaffold that blocks first impulses may favour value-maximising answers on decision tasks.

source: Campitelli & Labollita (2010) Correlations of cognitive reflection with judgments and choices
finding: Partial replication of Frederick in Argentina. CRT scores were much lower. CRT correlated with risk taking when the gamble had higher expected value, and with all estimation measures in correspondence tasks (city populations, geography, chess ratings). The authors say CRT is a broader thinking disposition, close to actively open-minded thinking.
numbers: N=157. CRT mean 0.80 (SD .92) men and .59 (SD .91) women, versus Frederick's 1.47 and 1.03; the sex gap was not significant (t(155)=1.36, p=.175). CRT with risk taking at higher expected value r(155)=.258, p=.0011. CRT with geographic knowledge r=.446. Chess ratings placed correctly in 13.0% of cases versus 10% by chance (t(156)=6.6).
limits: Frederick's finding that women commit more intuitive errors was not supported. Single sample, paper-and-pencil.
agent_relevance: The same test gives very different base rates by sample, so a cutoff for 'reflective' is population-bound. Check any threshold on our own item class.

source: Sinayev & Peters (2015) Cognitive reflection vs. calculation in decision making
finding: A boundary-condition result. CRT answers were modelled as two steps: noticing the intuition is wrong (Cognitive Reflection) and calculating the right answer (numeric ability). Numeric ability predicted better decisions; Cognitive Reflection added no independent prediction.
numbers: Study 1: N=1,413 (US panel, 2014) with 5 CRT items. Study 2: N=1,478 (18 dropped for inattention). Framing consistency: Cognitive Reflection r=-0.12 (p<.001), but in regression Cognitive Reflection b=-0.01 (p=.81) while numeracy b=-0.16 (p=.002). Calculation varied more (2.1) than Cognitive Reflection (1.2).
quote: Cognitive Reflection contributed no independent predictive power.
limits: Observational; depends on the two-step model. The authors say it is unclear if the lack of unique effect for Cognitive Reflection reflects a weak construct or low reliability.
agent_relevance: The CRT link to decision quality may be about skill, not about overriding. 'More checking' will not help if the checker lacks the skill to calculate. Pair override with a real tool (code).

source: Gangemi, Bourgeois-Gironde & Mancini (2015) Feelings of error in reasoning - in search of a phenomenon
finding: Adds the complement of feeling of rightness: a feeling of error (FOE) that arises when the reasoner detects conflict. In the bat-and-ball task, FOE was higher on the standard version (wrong answers) than on an isomorphic control, and lower in people who solved the standard problem. Study 1 asked people to generate an answer; Study 2 to choose between a normative and an intuitive answer.
numbers: Study 1: standard vs control F(1,101)=658.46, partial eta squared .87; correct solvers FOE M=8.79 (SD 4.51) vs wrong solvers M=16.52 (SD 4.95), F(1,143)=66.29, partial eta squared .32. Study 2: F(1,96)=424.02, partial eta squared .81; correct M=11.3 vs wrong M=14.18, F(1,146)=6.55, p<.02.
limits: Self-report questionnaire; the large first effect partly reflects different problem versions, not reasoning alone. Sample sizes are inferred from degrees of freedom only.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that a conflict signal exists and tracks correctness, but it is a human self-report. For us the signal must be code-computed (disagreement between attempts), not a self-rating.

source: Pennycook, Fugelsang & Koehler (2015) What makes us think? A three-stage dual-process model of analytic engagement
finding: A staged account. Stage 1: several Type 1 outputs are cued. Stage 2: conflict detection between them. Stage 3: if conflict is found, Type 2 either rationalises the Type 1 output (post-hoc check) or decouples from it (falsifies it). Bias comes from failures at either detection or decoupling, so the two are separable.
numbers: Core measure: reaction time on incongruent (stereotype vs base-rate conflict) minus congruent items. Rapid-response base-rate task, base rates such as 995/5.
quote: conflict detection and decoupling are dissociable sources of Type 2 processing
limits: Model argued from 4 experiments in one paradigm (base-rate problems, undergraduates).
agent_relevance: Maps to our schema: detection (S4 check or agreement test) is separate from repair (S5 revise). Failures can happen at either, so log them separately.

source: Pennycook, Fugelsang & Koehler (2015) What makes us think? A three-stage dual-process model of analytic engagement
finding: Experiment 1: undergraduates showed the RT increase on conflict items for both stereotype and base-rate answers, matching earlier work. Less biased people took less time when they overrode (efficient decoupling). A minority did not detect conflict at all.
numbers: N=62 (groups analysed 58-60). Congruent vs incongruent: base-rate responses t(59)=7.65, d=.99; stereotype responses t(57)=5.72, d=.75. RT increase for base-rate answers was 562 ms (about double). 17.2% of the sample took longer on congruent than incongruent items. The share of base-rate answers on incongruent items was .28 to .49 across conditions (Table 1).
limits: Detection failure is a minority pattern in this task. The authors warn the extra analytic time is small (about half a second). Part of the sample was reported in an earlier paper.
agent_relevance: Decoupling in this task is cheap. Do not expect a large reasoning cost to signal that an override happened; use a measurable disagreement.

source: Pennycook, Fugelsang & Koehler (2015) What makes us think? A three-stage dual-process model of analytic engagement
finding: Experiments 2 to 4 manipulated the cues. Extreme base rates (995/5) raised the conflict-detection effect for stereotype answers but did not change the time for overriding. Showing base rates before the stereotype lowered the detection effect and raised the decoupling effect. This is a double dissociation. Analytic thinking disposition went with the detection effect, not the decoupling effect.
numbers: Stereotype-answer RT cost: 598 ms with extreme base rates versus 120 ms with moderate base rates. Base-rate answer RT cost: 717 ms (extreme) versus 692 ms (moderate). Disposition-detection correlation r=.28 (p=.03, N=60) with moderate base rates.
limits: Order and extremity effects are specific to this task. Effects are in milliseconds and rely on a rapid-response format.
agent_relevance: Presentation order and signal strength change whether a conflict is noticed. Our restate step should present the competing cue explicitly, since weak conflict signals are missed.

source: Trippas, Thompson & Handley (2017) When fast logic meets slow belief: Evidence for a parallel-processing model of belief bias
finding: Tests DI against a parallel model of belief bias. Participants judged either validity or believability of the same conclusions. DI predicts belief should be quicker and should interfere with logic more than the reverse. For simpler problems (modus tollens) interference was symmetric, which fits parallel processing, not strict DI. For modus ponens belief was hurt slightly more than logic.
numbers: Experiment 1: N=45 (2 removed). Accuracy conflict .68 vs no-conflict .92. Modus ponens: conflict cost .30 under belief and .24 under logic. Modus tollens: .24 vs .17, no interaction. RT conflict 4786 ms vs no-conflict 4503 ms (d=0.17).
limits: Small effects; student samples; abstract problem contents. The asymmetry in accuracy was not seen in response times.
agent_relevance: Fast logic exists for simple items: the correct pass can be as quick as the heuristic pass. Do not assume a heuristic answer is always first.

source: Trippas, Thompson & Handley (2017) When fast logic meets slow belief: Evidence for a parallel-processing model of belief bias
finding: Experiment 2 raised complexity (syllogisms). For simple syllogisms interference was symmetric; for the complex three-term multiple-model syllogisms belief disturbed logic judgments far more than the reverse. This is the complexity moderation: parallel at low complexity, belief-dominated at high complexity.
numbers: N=84. Accuracy: belief instructions .80 vs logic instructions .71 overall. Complex, conflict items: .76 under belief vs .50 under logic; complex no-conflict .85 vs .71. Conflict x instruction: logic cost .21 vs belief cost .09 on complex items (p=.03). RT logic 10,718 ms vs belief 8,217 ms (d=0.42); conflict 9,584 vs no-conflict 9,188 ms (d=.06).
limits: The authors note simple syllogisms may be solvable with simple heuristics. Power simulation said d=0.20 was detectable.
agent_relevance: Item complexity decides whether the cheap pass is reliable. A difficulty estimate at the gate (S0) should route complex items to the checked path.

source: Bago & De Neys (2017) Fast logic?: Examining the time course assumption of dual process theory
finding: The key test of the DI time course, using the two-response paradigm: give a first answer fast (deadline and load to block Type 2), then a final answer. DI predicts wrong first, then correct. Instead, many correct final answers were already correct as the first answer, with high confidence and short latency, even when a heuristic answer competed.
numbers: 4 experiments, base-rate and syllogism tasks: Exp 1 N=101 (instructions only), Exp 2 N=104 (deadline), Exp 3 N=99 (load), Exp 4 N=115 (deadline + load). Final correct on conflict items: base-rate 40.1% avg, syllogisms 47.9% avg; no-conflict 94.1% and 76.9%. Of final correct conflict answers, 74.8% (base-rate) and 87.6% (syllogisms) were already correct at first response.
quote: fast and automatic Type 1 processing also cues a correct logical response from the start
limits: Crowd-sourced adults. 'Fast' is inferred from deadline and load. Many people still follow the DI path.
agent_relevance: The hardest case for 'slow thinking improves answers': the first pass is often already right. Pay for slow checking only when the first pass is not already right (G1, G11).

source: Bago & De Neys (2017) Fast logic?: Examining the time course assumption of dual process theory
finding: Direction-of-change table for conflict items (first answer then final answer: 00 wrong-wrong, 11 right-right, 01 wrong-right, 10 right-wrong). The 00 pattern was most common but 11 was large; correction of a wrong first answer (01) was uncommon. Load did not reduce 11, so correct first answers did not need extra Type 2 time.
numbers: Averages across the 4 experiments. Base rate: 11 = 30%, 00 = 56.7%, 10 = 3.2%, 01 = 10.1%. Syllogisms: 11 = 42.3%, 00 = 48.1%, 10 = 3.6%, 01 = 6.0%. Syllogism 11 under load rose (Exp 3 46.2%, Exp 4 49.7%) vs Exp 1 35.1%; chi-square(5)=12.07, p=.007.
limits: The 01 cells were assigned by arithmetic because the PDF table text was jumbled; totals match: 30+10.1=40.1% final-correct for base-rate.
agent_relevance: Revision rate (01) is only 6-10% while 10 (spoiling a right answer) is about 3%. Revisions are not free: gate the revise step so it does not turn right answers wrong.

source: Boissin, Caparos, Voudouri & De Neys (2022) Debiasing System 1: Training favours logical over stereotypical intuiting
finding: Short training that explains the logic of base-rate and conjunction problems raised accuracy at the first, load-limited answer, not just after deliberation. After training most people solved conflict problems right from the start. The gain lasted at least two months. Intuitions are trainable, not fixed.
numbers: Base-rate Study 1A: initial accuracy before training 39.6% control / 27.0% training; training gain +48.3 points vs +6.2 control; Block x Group F(1,99)=36.17, p<.001. '00' down 32.5%, '11' up 48.0%. No-conflict: 96.2% initial, 97.4% final. Conjunction Study 2A: final accuracy pre 9.7% control / 4.5% training; gain +58.3 vs +4.2 (F(1,98)=72.25, p<.001, generalized eta squared .21); '00' down 53.1%, '11' up 51.4%. No-conflict 77.6% initial, 79.4% final.
limits: The two-month retest used only the training group (final base-rate accuracy 80.6% at retest, lower than right after training). Conflict-detection results differed between the two tasks. Missed-deadline trials (3.5% and 2.0%) and failed load-task trials (12.9% and 9.2%) were dropped.
agent_relevance: The agent can move correct reasoning into the first pass by examples: worked solutions of the same problem class given in context raise first-pass accuracy. This matches the LLM few-shot result (a25).

source: Cited in opened papers: Thompson, Prowse Turner & Pennycook (2011); De Neys & Glumicic (2008); De Neys (2012)
finding: Cited in Trippas et al. 2017 and Pennycook et al. 2015, not read directly. Conflict items take longer and lower confidence than no-conflict items even when the person answers wrongly (De Neys & Glumicic 2008). Feeling of rightness predicts how long a person rethinks and whether they change the answer (Thompson et al. 2011). These are the base of the logical-intuition view.
numbers: No numbers were read for these sources. Do not cite figures from this line.
limits: Citation-only evidence. Read the originals for numbers before using.
agent_relevance: Basis for using agreement and confidence signals as a trigger, but only after we confirm them in code.

source: Sloman (1996) The empirical case for two systems of reasoning
finding: Proposes an associative system (similarity and contiguity) and a rule-based system running in parallel. Criterion S (simultaneous contradictory belief) is the evidence for two systems. Known only through Osman (2004) and Evans & Stanovich (2013); the full paper could not be fetched this session.
numbers: No numbers read from the original.
limits: Do not quote from this line; described second-hand only.
agent_relevance: The parallel-competitive model: both outputs exist and conflict is resolved. This is the design behind running a fast and a checked answer and comparing them.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: 150 CRT-style tasks (3 types) and semantic illusions given to GPT-1 up to GPT-4 and to 500 humans. Early models gave atypical answers; then models up to GPT-3-davinci gave the intuitive (trap) answer far more often than humans; ChatGPT and GPT-4 reversed this. The authors read the trap answers as System-1-like.
numbers: Intuitive (wrong) rate 70-90% for the GPT-3-davinci family vs 55% for humans. Correct: GPT-3-davinci-003 5%, humans 38%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, GPT-4 96%. Intuitive rate: ChatGPT-3.5 15%, GPT-4 0%, davinci-003 80%. Semantic illusions: davinci-003 fell for them 72% of the time (18% correct); ChatGPT-3.5 74% correct, GPT-4 88%. 500 Prolific humans (45 excluded for using external help).
limits: Tasks were built by the authors, but CRT-like items may be in the training data of newer models. Calling next-token output 'System 1' is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Per-model baselines differ: older models take the trap by default, newer ones do not. Test the scaffold against each model's plain baseline (G7); do not assume the model falls for CRT traps.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Chain-of-thought is the LLM counterpart of System 2. Adding 'Let's use algebra' to davinci-003 gave chain-of-thought in 100% of responses and cut trap answers. Removing chain-of-thought from ChatGPT models ('shortest possible answer') barely hurt: ChatGPT-3.5 correct unchanged, GPT-4 correct fell 95% to 88%. So newer models solve most CRT items without visible reasoning.
numbers: davinci-003 correct rose 5% to 28% with the algebra prompt (atypical answers rose 15% to 43%). Chain-of-thought rate for ChatGPT-3.5 fell from 97% to 0% and GPT-4 from 84% to 0%; GPT-4 intuitive responses rose from 0% to 10%.
limits: Single task family; the 'no reasoning' prompt may leave hidden computation inside the model.
agent_relevance: For easy, familiar items extra visible reasoning adds little; reserve long reasoning for hard or novel items (G11). Short-answer plain mode is a valid strong baseline.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Examples fix the fast pass in LLMs, as training does in humans. Giving davinci-003 correct solutions of similar tasks in the prompt lifted accuracy; a care instruction also helped on semantic illusions.
numbers: CRT Type 2: 2% to 92% after two examples. CRT Type 3: 12% to 92% after seven examples. Semantic illusions: 'Think carefully and check the question for invalid assumptions' raised correct 18% to 54% (intuitive 72% to 28%); with 10 or more worked examples correct reached over 64%.
limits: Examples were of the same type; transfer to different item types was not read here.
agent_relevance: Few-shot worked cases for the same item class are cheap and strong. Put class-matched solved examples into the first attempt before adding extra thinking loops.

source: Wason & Evans (1974) Dual processes in reasoning?; Evans & Over (1996) Rationality and reasoning
finding: Founding result for the heuristic-analytic split: on the Wason selection task people choose cards matching the words in the rule (matching bias) and their stated reasons justify the choice after the fact. Known here only through Osman (2004) and Evans & Stanovich (2013), not opened.
numbers: No numbers read from the original papers.
limits: Do not quote from this line.
agent_relevance: Post-hoc justification of a heuristic choice is the human version of G10: reasoning text is not evidence of cause.

source: Kahneman & Frederick (2002) Representativeness revisited: attribute substitution in intuitive judgment
finding: Attribute substitution: when a target question is hard, the mind answers an easier related one (for example, similarity for probability) and System 2 monitors and may endorse it. Known here through Evans & Stanovich (2013) only; the original was not opened.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Models also substitute: they answer a similar known problem. Restating the problem (S1) and testing against a variant (G3) are the checks.
